newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl sets out Europe goal for monetary union.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl sets out Europe goal for monetary union.

text.p: German chancellor Helmut Kohl, widely seen as the driving force behind European integration, said on Friday that Europe's goal had to be to get as many fully-qualified countries into monetary union as possible in 1999.
In a speech to the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt, Kohl said, "The goal must be that many nations meet the stability criteria and participate in the currency union from the beginning."

Finance ministers also addressing the gathering of some 800 bankers reaffirmed their commitment to creating a stable European currency on time in 1999 and said they were determined their countries would be in at the start.

Italy's Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said his country was making every effort to be a founder member of Economic and Monetary Union and stressed that Italy wanted to be a respected, stable member of the planned currency union.
He told the 800 bankers at the congress that Italy wanted to be see as an element of stability and "not of distortion".
"Italy intends to be one of the founding members of the EMU", he said. "Italians are determined to do everything necessary to be an element of stability and not an element of tension or distortion".

Spain's Economy Minister, Rodrigo de Rato, said, "I believe by now there ought not to be many doubts...in financial markets that Spain finds itself on the right track to convergence and monetary union".

European countries which want to meld their currencies in the planned Euro from 1999 are scrambling to meet economic targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt in the 1997 year.

Most European countries are facing the greatest problems in meeting the fiscal targets, which call for budget deficits to run at a maximum of three percent of gross domestic product and public debt at a maximum of 60 percent of GDP.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis brushed aside worries that France's bid to cut its budget deficits to meet the Maastricht goal in 1997 was only a one-off effort.
"This effort is part of a strategy to cut the public deficit on a durable basis," he said.
Arthuis stressed that France intended to achieve long-term fiscal stability, adding that such discipline will be essential for the stability of the future European currency.
The French budget deficit would be within the three percent limit in 1997. France then intended to cut the deficit to 2.8 percent in 1998 and to below two percent by the year 2001.

Ciampi, reaffirming Italy's commitment to the integration process, said he would be seeking to put the Italian lira back into Europe's exchange rate mechanism in November, a key step in making Italy eligible for entry to the European currency.
Most analysts have been expecting the lira, which crashed out of the ERM in 1992, to return to the mechanism in time for the European Union's Dublin summit on December 13-14.
But aside from their commitment to the economic goals, the ministers also demonstrated that they were clearly dedicated to the vision of an integrated Europe.

Ruairi Quinn, Irish Finance Minister and president of the European council of finance ministers, said that Europe ought to be able to achieve its goals even if some countries -- a thinly veiled reference to Britain -- remained sceptical.
